# In Defense of the Wrong Turn

There is a particular kind of knowledge that belongs to people who have taken wrong turns. They know which stations smell faintly of iron, which towns offer a different kind of coffee at four in the afternoon, and how to enter an unfamiliar neighborhood without feeling that every corner is accusing them of incompetence. Most of us receive this education accidentally, usually as children, when the adults responsible for us are busy with tickets, maps, or the confident assumption that they know where they are going. We wander. We notice. We remember and carry those accidental lessons into adulthood, disguised as stories.

Years later, the destination matters less than the detour. I once missed a bus in a city I cannot name and, with nothing to do but wait, followed a road because its awnings were the color of mandarins. The road climbed. A bakery appeared, then a row of houses with blue doors, then a tiny park where a man was reading three newspapers at once. I arrived at the correct stop twenty minutes late, carrying an improbable account of a cat wearing a red collar and a fountain that seemed to be operated by an invisible hand. The delay was inconvenient. The memory is still bright.

This is one of the quiet rewards of being lost: the world stops being a diagram and becomes specific. A planned visit often emphasizes the monument, the museum, the famous café. An unplanned one includes the laundromat where you change a bill, the locked gate with vines growing through it, the elderly woman feeding sparrows from a paper bag. These details were always there, but urgency made them invisible. Getting lost slows us down enough to receive them. It asks nothing more dramatic than that we pay attention. That may seem a small thing, until you remember how rarely you have done it.

Try an experiment sometime. Put on comfortable shoes, leave your phone in your pocket, and walk in a direction that does not particularly interest you. Do not aim to arrive anywhere impressive. Turn when a street looks quiet, not when it looks efficient. Notice the weather changing from one block to the next: a strip of sun, the metallic chill of an alley, rain beginning against a drainpipe. Within half an hour, the familiar city will have loosened its grip. You are no longer a traveler passing through. You are a temporary resident, subject to the same crooked chimneys, mismatched chairs, and sleepy dogs as everyone else.

Attention, in this way, resembles affection. We do not love a person merely because we know where they live or what they do on Sundays. We love them through the accumulation of unremarkable particulars: the song they hum while cooking, the way they leave their keys in strange bowls, the story they tell slightly differently each time. A place becomes lovable in much the same way. The route you take to the bus can matter more than the destination if the route contains a bakery window clouded with steam, a lover’s graffiti, or a tree that blooms every spring beside an iron gate.

Getting lost also teaches a useful form of humility. The first time you realize that everyone else may know where they are going, and you do not, can be uncomfortable. Then, paradoxically, it can be liberating. When the destination no longer commands you, small possibilities return. Take the long way home. Buy lunch from the place with the handwritten menu. Read the book with the dull title; it may turn out to contain the sentence you needed. Many good things enter our lives disguised as bad plans. That is not an argument for wasting time, but for allowing time to surprise you.

Science, history, and art are all built from the ability to be wrong without surrendering to error. A wrong answer can be an invitation to look again. The old models are not shameful; they are records of questions asked with the tools available at the time. The awkward theories, discarded maps, failed experiments, and abandoned manuscripts form a kind of negative architecture, showing us not just what we know but how knowledge was made. To be wrong, then, is not to be defeated. It is to stand at the border of the known and remain curious long enough to see what is beyond it.

The same principle applies to conversation. Certain people make us feel that every uncertain thought must be hidden quickly, lest they mistake it for weakness. Other people create room around a question, a hesitation, a change of mind. We reveal ourselves most honestly in these intervals, between the certainty we have prepared and the certainty we have not. A good friend does not need us to be interesting at every moment. They make it possible to be provisional, to say, “I used to think so,” or “I have no idea,” without treating either phrase as a failure of hospitality. Sometimes the shortest route between two people is not a direct statement, but a shared silence.

We should be careful, however, not to romanticize every wrong turn. Some detours are simply detours. Some roads flood, some plans waste money, and some lost directions put us in danger. A taste for wandering is not an excuse to ignore signs, weather, or the advice of people who know the terrain. The point is not to make inefficiency into a virtue. The point is to leave a small door open in a life dominated by efficiency.

There is a technology of orientation: the sun, a silhouette, a chimney, the direction of water in a stream. Skills our ancestors used survive in us as instincts, sleeping until we need them. On a map, a route is a line. In memory, it is a chain of sensations: wet pavement, a chestnut, the sound of bells. We do not remember where we went. We remember who we were when we went there—and that, perhaps, is the thing about wandering.

"Science, history, and art are all built from the ability to be wrong without surrendering to error. A wrong answer can be an invitation to look again.
